title: Loss aversion: why you hold losers
desc: Why a loss hurts twice as much, and how that feeling moves your stop

cards.title: A fair coin flip
cards.situation: Heads, you win $100. Tails, you lose $100. The coin is fair. Most people say no to this bet. Why?

options.feedback: A fair coin gives even odds. People refuse because the loss would hurt more than the win would please.

options.text: Losing $100 feels worse than winning $100 feels good
options.feedback: That’s loss aversion. Studies find a loss hurts about twice as much as an equal gain feels good.

options.text: The bet is too small to bother
options.feedback: Size isn’t the reason: people turn down small fair bets too. The loss would hurt more than the win would please.

cards.work: 50% × +$100 and 50% × −$100: on average, $0. The odds are even. The feelings are not.

cards.title: Losses hurt about twice as much
cards.text: This is **[[loss-aversion|loss aversion]]**. To dodge the pain, you’re tempted to hold losers so you never have to “make it real”, and to sell winners early to feel the win.

visual.label: Winning $100 feels like ×1; losing $100 feels like ×2

blocks.tip: The feeling is normal. Letting it move your stop is the mistake.

cards.title: Hope is not a stop
cards.text: Say you buy at $50 with a stop at $47. Price hits $47. You move the stop to $45, then $42, then remove it.

chart.label: Bought at $50; price breaks the $47 stop and falls to $38

blocks.tip: You finally sell at $38. Planned loss: about $3 a share. Actual loss: $12. Four times the plan.

cards.title: Is it a loss yet?
cards.myth: It’s not a loss until I sell.
cards.reality: The loss is real now. Your money is stuck in a losing trade either way. Not selling only hides it from you.
cards.text: Ask: “Would I buy this today, at this price?” If not, why hold it? The stop decides, not hope.

cards.title: The stop is hit
cards.q: You bought 100 shares at $40, stop at $37. Price hits $37. You think “it’ll come back”. What now?

options.feedback: Moving the stop is hope, not a plan. Each move makes the possible loss bigger.

options.text: Let the stop sell and take the loss
options.feedback: That’s the plan working: a small loss, taken on purpose, as you decided before the trade.

options.text: Buy more to lower your average price
options.feedback: Buying more makes a losing trade bigger right when your plan says it’s wrong.
With no stop, a planned $300 loss has no limit. Hope is not a stop.

cards.work: $3 × 100 shares = about a $300 loss, as planned. A gap can make it a bit more.

options.feedback: Losses happen to every trader. Loss aversion is about how much they hurt, not how often they come.

options.text: A loss feels about twice as bad as an equal gain feels good
options.feedback: Losses sting about twice as much, which tempts you to avoid taking them.
Every trader takes losses. Loss aversion is the extra pain they cause, which tempts you to avoid taking them.

options.text: Losers should be held until they recover
options.feedback: That’s the mistake loss aversion tempts you into, not what it means.

cards.headline: You can take a small loss on purpose.
lines: A loss hurts about twice as much as a gain feels good.
A loss is real before you sell.
The stop decides, not hope. Never move it further away.
